62098.etyen:
PIE word
 *gʷḗn
Compound of trell (“thrall, slave”) + kvinne (“woman”), literally “thrall woman”.
The first element, trell (“thrall, slave”), is from Old Norse þræll (“thrall, slave”), from Proto-Germanic *þragilaz (“runner, servant”), with several alternative reconstructions. Its deeper origin is uncertain, though it is commonly connected with a Germanic verb meaning “to run”.
The second element, kvinne (“woman”), is from Old Norse kvinna (“woman”), also kvenna, probably back-formed from the genitive plural of kona (“woman, wife”), from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ (“woman”), ultimately from Proto-I

Borrowed from Swedish å (“the letter å”). The letter was introduced into official Norwegian orthography in 1917, replacing the traditional Danish–Norwegian digraph ⟨aa⟩.
The character originated as an early modern German typographical innovation and entered Swedish through the printing press, appearing in works including Olaus Petri's catechism and the Swedish New Testament of 1526. Graphically, it developed from ⟨aa⟩, with the second ⟨a⟩ written above the first and gradually reduced to a ring.
The digraph and later the letter represented the development of Old Norse long á /ɑː/, which became  / Inherited from Old Norse á (“stream, river”), from Proto-Germanic *ahwō (“stream, river; water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂ (“water”).
Cognate with Icelandic á, Faroese á, Swedish å, Danish å, Old English ēa and German Ache (“stream, river”). / Derived from Swedish Å (“the letter Å”). 1001106.etyen:
Borrowed from Latin Iōnās (“male given name and biblical name”), from Ancient Greek Ἰωνᾶς (Iōnâs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹנָה (Yōnā, “dove”). The final ⟨s⟩ reflects the Greek and Latin nominative forms. The surname is derived from the given name.
Compare Danish Jonas, Swedish Jonas, Icelandic Jónas and Faroese Jónas (“male given name”).

1004946.etyen:
anorakk (“anorak”) + lomme (“pocket”), literally “anorak pocket”. The first element, anorakk, ultimately reflects Greenlandic annoraaq (“anorak, fur overall”), from Proto-Inuit *atnuʀaaq (“clothing”), ultimately connected with Proto-Eskimo *atə- (“to put on”), although the precise formation of the Proto-Inuit word is uncertain. The second element, lomme (“pocket”), is of uncertain origin; compare Danish lomme, West Frisian lomme, and dialectal Swedish lomma.
Compare the parallel formation Danish anoraklomme (“anorak pocket”).
